True  Both traditional single-principal-element tungsten alloys and multiple-principal-element refractory HEAs face significant challenges in achieving high ductility due to the formation of brittle secondary phases, though the specific phase types and underlying design limitations differ. Traditional approaches for tungsten alloys rely on dilute concentrations of alloying elements within a single principal-element system [PMC10213035::reader_question::a82b8545bc904f84::answer::ed6d90c68fb347ce]. In contrast, the refractory HEA paradigm utilizes multiple principal elements to incorporate nano-precipitates, aiming to improve both strength and ductility [PMC10213035::reader_question::662e75fa7cf635fc::answer::0eee67ade85e7ab4]. Refractory HEAs exhibit limited tensile ductility primarily at ambient temperatures due to the formation of intrinsically brittle intermetallic phases like silicides, B2, and Laves phases [PMC10213035::reader_question::662e75fa7cf635fc::answer::0eee67ade85e7ab4]. There is no direct contradiction between the answers; rather, they delineate different regimes of failure. The text clarifies that the multiple-principal-element paradigm does not *inherently* solve the stability issues found in nickel-base superalloys or traditional W alloys because refractory HEAs are prone to the formation of brittle secondary phases (silicides, B2, Laves) that limit ductility [PMC10213035::reader_question::662e75fa7cf635fc::answer::0eee67ade85e7ab4], whereas the failure in traditional W alloys is specifically attributed to W-enriched bcc phases [PMC10213035::reader_question::a82b8545bc904f84::answer::ed6d90c68fb347ce]. The fundamental difference in stability lies in the phase formation thermodynamics: single-principal-element W alloys fail due to W-enrichment in the bcc matrix, while refractory HEAs fail due to the thermodynamic instability of complex intermetallics (silicides, B2, Laves) that precipitate in multi-component systems at ambient temperatures.
